summary: Extends the general Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) mechanisms, such as tracing, bypass, and callouts, so they work for HTTP traffic. Together with the generic OPES documents, this profile forms a complete specification for adapting HTTP messages using services at the network edge. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a helper in the middle of the road changes a parcel on its way, like adding a stamp. This memo explains how such helpers can safely work on web traffic.

questions: how does opes work with http
how does opes adapt http messages
what is an opes callout server
subtitle: How a helper server at the edge of the network is told which parts of an HTTP message to adapt, and how the result stays valid HTTP.

tldr.problem: The generic OPES callout protocol does not know anything about HTTP, so an OPES processor and a callout server need agreed rules for handing HTTP headers, bodies and trailers back and forth.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4236 defines two HTTP profiles (request and response) with six named message parts, a few extra negotiation parameters, two new OCP message parameters, and the OPES-System, OPES-Via and OPES-Bypass headers for tracing and bypass.
tldr.outcome: Together with the application-agnostic OPES documents, it forms a complete specification for HTTP adaptation with OPES. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4236 is a Proposed Standard from November 2005, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be read together with the generic OPES documents such as RFC 4037 and RFC 3897.

sections.title: Scope and the OPES Document Map
sections.content:
The Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) framework describes application-agnostic mechanisms, such as the OPES callout protocol (RFC 4037) and OPES entity communications (RFC 3897). RFC 4236 extends those mechanisms for one specific application protocol, HTTP.

The RFC says that the generic OPES documents plus this HTTP profile form a complete specification for HTTP adaptation with OPES. It also includes a map of the other OPES documents, such as the architecture (RFC 3835), use cases (RFC 3752) and the risk analysis (RFC 3837), because OPES documents are hard to understand in isolation.

At the core of OPES are two network elements: the OPES processor and the callout server. They talk to each other using the OPES Callout Protocol (OCP). This RFC says how that conversation works when the thing being adapted is an HTTP message.
sections.eli5: There is a general rule book for helpers that change things in transit. This memo is the chapter about web traffic.

sections.title: Message Parts and the Two Profiles
sections.content:
An HTTP message has well-known parts: headers, a body and trailers. RFC 4236 names six am-part values (application message parts): request-header, request-body, request-trailer, response-header, response-body and response-trailer. A header part includes the start-line, all headers and the blank line that ends them.

The RFC defines two profiles, each with its own feature identifier. In the request profile, the processor sends request parts, and the callout server sends back either adapted request parts or adapted response parts, never both. Sending response parts lets the server short-circuit the transaction, for example to answer a forbidden request without forwarding it. In the response profile, the processor sends response parts, and the request parts may be offered as auxiliary parts.

Parts must be sent in the order the profile lists them. An agent MUST NOT send a part that the profile does not allow, and an agent that receives one MUST terminate the transaction with an error. Absent parts (a request with no body, a message with no trailer) are simply skipped. Unless configured otherwise, an OPES processor MUST offer all non-auxiliary original parts.
sections.eli5: A web message is like a letter with an envelope, the letter itself and sometimes a note at the end. The rules say which pieces get handed to the helper and in what order.

sections.title: Negotiating Profile Parameters
sections.content:
An HTTP profile is a feature in an OCP Negotiation Offer (NO), answered by a Negotiation Response (NR). Its scope is the OCP connection by default, or a service group named with the SG parameter. The profile adds five optional parameters.

  • Aux-Parts: the processor lists auxiliary parts it could add (such as the original request headers in a response profile), and the server replies with the subset it wants. The server MUST NOT pick a part that was not offered.
  • Pause-At-Body: the server asks the processor to pause sending the body at a given offset, as if a Want Data Paused message had been received.
  • Stop-Receiving-Body: the server says it wants no more of the body after a given offset, as if a Want Stop Receiving Data message had been received.
  • Preservation-Interest-Body: the size of a body prefix the server may send back unchanged, which lets the processor optimize what it keeps.
  • Content-Encodings: the server's preferred content codings, most preferred first. The processor MUST NOT bypass a service just because the actual encoding does not match.

The RFC's worked example offers the request-header and request-body as auxiliary parts for service group 5. The server asks only for request-header, sets Pause-At-Body to 30, Preservation-Interest-Body to 0 and Content-Encodings to (gzip).
sections.eli5: Before work starts, the helper and the mail room agree on extras: which extra pieces the helper wants to see, when to take a break, and which wrapping it likes best.

sections.title: Carrying HTTP Messages in OCP
sections.content:
Two OCP messages gain a new parameter. The Application Message Start (AMS) message may carry AM-EL, the entity length of the body before any transfer codings. An agent that knows the exact length SHOULD announce it, and MUST NOT send AM-EL if the length is unknown. Wrong lengths can have drastic consequences for the recipient.

Every Data Use Mine (DUM) message in an HTTP transaction MUST carry an AM-Part parameter naming exactly one part. A part can be split across several DUM messages with the same AM-Part.

HTTP transfer encodings are hop-by-hop. Unless they are explicitly negotiated, which this RFC does not describe, an OCP agent MUST NOT send transfer-encoded bodies. The processor MUST remove the Transfer-Encoding header before sending headers to the callout server, and MUST send a correct one to the next HTTP recipient itself. Other hop-by-hop headers MAY be forwarded to callout servers.

The profile applies to all HTTP messages, including 1xx responses and requests such as POST, CONNECT and OPTIONS. Unless configured otherwise, an OPES processor MUST forward all HTTP messages for adaptation. The RFC warns that skipping 'control' messages can cause security flaws: for example, a malicious CONNECT request might not get logged.
sections.eli5: Each piece of the web message is handed over with a label saying which piece it is. Nobody is allowed to skip a piece just because it looks boring.

sections.title: Keeping the HTTP Message Correct
sections.content:
A callout server may change a body without fixing the headers. So an OPES processor MUST ensure that all computable headers, meaning those whose value can be worked out from the body alone, are correct before it sends the message on. The RFC names Content-Length and Content-MD5. A processor must not trust the Content-Length it gets from a callout server by default.

For the message size, the RFC lists a preference order, with closing the connection as the last resort:

  1. If the server sent AM-EL, use it to create Content-Length and keep a persistent connection.
  2. Otherwise, if HTTP allows it, use chunked transfer encoding and remove any Content-Length.
  3. Otherwise, if the processor can wait for the transaction to finish, compute and add Content-Length.
  4. Otherwise, delete Content-Length, forward the data immediately and mark the end by closing the connection.

For Content-MD5, the processor MUST assume the checksum is now invalid. An HTTP intermediary that is not authoritative for the content MUST remove the header unless it detects that the message was not modified.
sections.eli5: If the helper changes the contents of a parcel, the weight and the stamp on the outside may be wrong. The mail room has to re-weigh and fix the label before sending it on.

sections.title: An Example: Blocking a Request
sections.content:
The RFC walks through several message flows. In the first, a user asks a proxy for the home page of www.restricted.example.com, and a URL-blocking service on the callout server denies it.

The processor and server exchange CS messages, the processor creates service group 11 and offers the request profile, and the server accepts. The processor then starts a transaction (TS), sends the request header in a DUM message and ends the message (AME). Instead of adapted request parts, the server answers with response parts: an AMS, a DUM carrying a 403 Forbidden header and a DUM with a short HTML body saying access is not allowed. This is the short-circuit described for the request profile.

The other examples show a language translation of a plain text response, where the processor sets AM-EL to 86 and the server replies with 78, and an HTML edit that uses data preservation (DUY and DPI messages) to send an unchanged header back cheaply.
sections.eli5: A visitor asks for a forbidden page. The helper says no and hands back a polite 'not allowed' note, so the request never goes any further.

sections.title: Tracing and Bypass Headers
sections.content:
To make adaptation visible, the RFC defines HTTP headers for the tracing and bypass mechanisms of RFC 3897. Trace entries go in OPES-System and OPES-Via; each entry is an agent identifier (an absolute URI) followed by optional parameters. An OPES System MUST add its entry to OPES-System, which is the only required tracing header. Other OPES agents use OPES-Via if they add entries. All agents MUST append their entries, so the headers show the order of changes.

Optional trace entries MAY go in a message trailer, but required ones MUST NOT. Agents SHOULD use a single header field for a long trace, because repeated equally named fields are illegal in HTTP and may not work with OPES-unaware proxies.

For bypass, the OPES-Bypass header can be added to HTTP requests. It carries either an asterisk, meaning all OPES agents, or a list of agent identifiers to bypass.
sections.eli5: Helpers sign a guest book on the parcel so the receiver can see who touched it. There is also a 'please do not touch' sticker a sender can add.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says that HTTP profiles do not introduce any HTTP-specific security considerations, since application-independent ones are covered in the application-agnostic OPES documents. It adds that this does not make HTTP adaptation immune to threats.

Two examples are given: rewriting the Request-URI of an HTTP CONNECT request, and removing a hop-by-hop Upgrade header before the HTTP proxy can act on it. OPES agents MUST NOT do such things without the consent of the HTTP client or server.
sections.eli5: A helper may not secretly change where a parcel is going or remove a note meant for someone else unless the sender or receiver agreed.
